title: The Disappearance of the Bronze Serpent
paragraphs:
The Disappearance of the Bronze Serpent
The Day Israel Destroyed a Miracle—and Why Millions Are Still Worshiping the Wrong Thing Today
There are moments in Scripture so shocking that they almost feel out of place.
Moments that force us to ask whether we have truly understood God at all.
The disappearance of the Bronze Serpent is one of those moments.
It was not buried by invading armies.
Reduced to pieces by God's own people.
And what makes this story even more startling is that the object being destroyed was once personally commanded by God Himself.
That fact alone should stop us in our tracks.
Because sometimes the greatest threat to our relationship with God is not rebellion.
Sometimes it is turning yesterday's blessing into today's idol.
The story begins in the wilderness.
Again and again God had delivered them, fed them, protected them, and guided them, yet they continued to complain.
Numbers 21 records one of their darkest moments.
The people spoke against God and against Moses.
As judgment, venomous serpents entered the camp.
The Hebrew text calls them הַנְּחָשִׁים הַשְּׂרָפִים (ha-nechashim ha-seraphim), literally "fiery serpents."
Suddenly the people realized the seriousness of their sin.
And God responded with a solution unlike anything anyone expected.
"Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live."
עֲשֵׂה לְךָ שָׂרָף וְשִׂים אֹתוֹ עַל־נֵס
"Asseh lecha saraph, vesim oto al nes."
"Make for yourself a fiery serpent and place it upon a standard."
The phrase itself is almost poetic.
Those who looked upon it in faith lived.
The bronze serpent possessed no power.
The miracle was never in the object.
The miracle was in trusting the word of God.
This becomes even more profound when Jesus Himself explains the event.
"And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life."
Καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσε τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ
"Kai kathos Mōysēs hypsōse ton ophin en tē erēmō."
"And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness..."
The bronze serpent was never the destination.
A living illustration pointing toward Christ.
The people looked in faith and lived.
Sinners would look to Christ and be saved.
The bronze serpent was never about a snake.
Yet human hearts have a tragic tendency.
We often fall in love with the sign and forget what it was pointing toward.
The very object God had once commanded remained among the people.
At first it may have been preserved as a reminder.
The people began treating the symbol as though it possessed power.
What was meant to point toward God began replacing God.
What was meant to strengthen faith became an object of misplaced faith.
The object that once represented healing became an idol.
One of the most faithful kings in Judah's history.
A man who loved the Lord.
A king unwilling to tolerate counterfeit worship.
And then Scripture records one of the most shocking acts of spiritual courage in all the Bible.

"He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan."
Most scholars understand it as something like:
For centuries people revered this object.
Perhaps some even believed it carried divine power.
Then Hezekiah looked at it and essentially said:
How many people must have protested?
"This has been with us for generations!"
Yet Hezekiah understood something many believers still struggle to grasp.
Anything that takes the place of God must go.
Even if God originally used it.
Sometimes even a past spiritual experience.
Things that once pointed us toward Christ.
Yet over time we begin trusting them more than we trust Jesus.
We defend them more passionately than we defend the Gospel.
We cling to them even when God is calling us forward.
They often arrive disguised as blessings.
The bronze serpent teaches us a painful but necessary lesson.
God is not interested in preserving our idols.
He is interested in preserving our hearts.
And sometimes the most loving thing God can do is allow the destruction of something we have elevated above Him.
Perhaps that is where you find yourself today.
Maybe something has disappeared from your life.
And you have been asking why.
Could it be that God is removing what you were tempted to worship so you can rediscover the One who deserves worship?
Because God has never shared His glory with idols.
The bronze serpent vanished because its purpose had been fulfilled.
Its role had always been temporary.
"Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and today, and forever."
Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς χθὲς καὶ σήμερον ὁ αὐτός καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας
"Iēsous Christos chthes kai sēmeron ho autos kai eis tous aiōnas."
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
That is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Because every human being carries a scandal.
Something that whispers they are too far gone.
Yet the cross announces a different verdict.
He takes what sin destroyed and transforms it through grace.
He takes shame and gives forgiveness.
He takes rebellion and offers reconciliation.
He takes brokenness and creates beauty.
He takes scandal and writes redemption.
That is exactly what the bronze serpent was pointing toward all along.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
Maybe today is the day you stop looking at the bronze serpent.
Maybe today is the day you stop trusting symbols and start trusting the Savior.
Maybe today is the day you surrender fully to Christ.
If this message stirred something inside your heart, do not keep scrolling.
This may have touched something deeper than you expected.
The most dangerous idol is often the one that once reminded you of God.
